I'm deeply thankful and honored to be given this opportunity to learn from the very best traders around. Took me a long time to find my way here. I started trading around 3 years ago as a price action trader (market structure, candle PA like pin bars. etc...) then immersed in the world of S/D trading (Sam Seiden) where I gained a new understanding of the market. But there was (or better still is) always a missing piece to truly understand the market. Sure, winning 38% of the times while trading S/D zones (TP 3R) let's you gain some pips but it is still a pain when you get the so often losing streak of 5-9 trades. I always knew that there was somewhere a better place to learn the mechanics of the markets, something that describes and show how everything works, in all time frames and where B.S. like "noise" is a fancy word for incompetence I don't believe in self-limits. Your perception becomes your reality. If you can think it, then you can achieve it. How often do you hear, predicting the market is not possible. Let alone the "it's all random" talk. This will be my small corner where I'll share my thoughts, understandings, doubts, progress and of course trades. Please feel always free to post any question, suggestion and criticism. Yes, which level is going to hold, the only trading question that matters. The journey for me to answer that question starts here and from the basics. So let's begin Disclaimer for this and all future posts: the following contents come from my own understanding of the original teachings by IF and other members, so always be aware that I could be totally wrong and that each unit of knowledge is subject to my own interpretation, filtering and may not reflect the original concepts as intended by IF Caps on price Every S/D trader knows them in and out, yet the best, strongest and perfect looking ones still fail. I can conclude from my own experience that the shape of the base and departure strength from a level have only limited influence on the overall outcome. What really matters, as RTM teaches, is the context. But before I get into that. There are some important clues that I consider to determine the quality of the base, I'm sure someone else here at RTM pointed them out. An interesting fact is that many traders think that consolidation (bases in RBD/RBD/RBR/DBD) means low activity (volume) and that momentum bars happen due to high volume. Sure, sometimes this is right, but most of the time momentum bars (liquidity gaps) are thin market moves (low volume) because price has to move in one direction once the last unfilled order is filled and ready to move to the next liquidity zone (base), where enough opposing orders get filled to stop price for some time, until again the balance gets broken one way or the other. This is also the reason why price bounces from those bases, because of unfilled orders left over from the last battle. S/D traders say that those orders at the bases are left there for undefined time, even for years. But it was a real revelation to me what RTM teaches about targets (PAZ). Another common reason for RBD/DBR failures is also explained by RTM. Just by knowing this and the above, we should be able to filter out many losses. Now to what really matters, the context where caps happen. Target 1 was there because of the past history: I see that in the last part I'm already ahead with FTRs, engulfs and targets. I will try to get in those in my next series of posts. And it is also clear from the above, that one concept taken in isolation (in this case price caps) is not enough to decipher price. ( price breaking into PAZ, by the truth, it breaks the last FTR before the PAZ, so simply enters the first one..., no breakings.. why we expect it will break all through ?.) That's because those are 2 different types of PAZs. Check out these two posts from Les_paul: post1 and post2 I think the SPAZ type works only if there is nothing important on the left, like a broken key level. Because the break of a key level makes it an FTR/FL. Also the reason for ITs creating stacked S/D is to pick up orders on the way and on return to fake out all classic S/D and S/R traders. Think about it this way, if ITs created those stacked demand/supply bases to fill their orders on the way, this means that on return there is little possibility of unfilled orders still left there. This is especially true for compression PAZs. That's why price needs to break only the last/first demand just before the CPAZ or SPAZ to make it through the entire zone. So if there are still unfilled orders then they are likely there at the tip (entrance of PAZ) and not inside that consumed zone. Report to moderator Quick Reply Reply Quote Thank You Jurij's Corner 12 Jun 2016 17:54 #232 Jurij Topic Author --> Offline Associate Trader Think in terms of frequency Posts: 557 Thank you received: 1348 althoufx wrote: [...] ......yes Jurji i remember those posts, also because LP said later to be not enough confident on this stuff for keeping trades based on this knowledge, then it looked like a topic not yet solved, as in stand-by conditions. So those posts were instead taken as pieces of the puzzle...am i wrong ? thanks for your reply !! Right, PAZs are just a piece of the puzzle like everything else. This is something that I think is the key to understand: 1. Some FL/FTRs work but many don't, so this concept is not enough on its own 2. Some engulfs work but many don't, so this concept is not enough on its own 3. PAZs (all types) work but many don't, so this concept is not enough on its own 4. QM/Diamond patterns work but many don't, so this concept is not enough on its own 5. Compression is sometimes a reversal sign but not always (LQ after compression is common) 6. S/D levels work but many don't 7. FO levels sometimes work but many don't ... I think it is clear where this is leading to. Perhaps this is exactly what IF means by saying that we need to make that final juxtaposition, where we see those concepts all at the same time. Often there is this common question in the homework section: "Why did that or this FTR/FL/CP/... fail?" Because it was never meant to work that way. Looking at the charts, there are almost dead sure setups that present itself only if multiple of the above RTM concepts appear together in the same setup. For example: at HTF supply, a trick is played (FO) then at the right shoulder of the trick level price forms an FTR/FL which happens to be a QM level also. Price meanwhile broke a lower FL and starts to retrace to the QM level. On approach price is starting to compress (making a CPAZ). Once price hits the QM FTR level at the FO key level at HTF supply price bounces and breaks into the CPAZ. If price now retraces back to the origin for a second chance entry then you have one of those almost dead sure trades Something like this past setup: Jurij wrote: CADJPY 30m Had a limit sell order not triggered, too high 5m LTF second chance (missed this one too) I think those setups are really nice and clear, that's what I want to trade more. I guess the difficulty in all this is to have the patience to wait and take only that kind of setups. Check this box to be notified of replies to this topic. First the charts As you can see price stopped at the first opposing FL of that scale (good for 1st profit tg). Then the pivot low 30m FL base, was not a good point for the full reversal. Reasons: 1. the base was a pivot low, which means a reaction to a previous base, in this case a 30m FTR (which itself is the top of a small CP) 2. the sharp arrival and departure makes this more a stop hunt/fake out than a full reversal, also because most reversals have larger tops with QM/diamond levels 3.this low (where my entry was) and the pivot low can be used by ITs for future tricks (FO), whereas that small 30m FTR looks absolutely not interesting to retail traders 4. the better entry can be seen on chart #2 after the new 1m engulf signal either at the 1m quasimodo level or at the origin of the engulf, with the stop below the ftr base, I started to doubt about the validity of that engulf, but in the end price reached the target FL above. The question remains as how far price can retrace before meeting it's original target after an engulf Attachments: Check this box to be notified of replies to this topic. All this drama happens in the big picture: From H4 supply to H4 demand (or lower... haven't checked). So basically you were buying where everyone was selling. Now you know. In one of the first post I wrote that for me a FL is a FTR of a previous FTR (something like an important FTR). Then I had a lot of trouble because of the markepedia FL page which shows FLs before a zone break (ie. FL without FTR). I would call those decision points rather than FLs. But now it is clear to me that there is no FL without FTR. And to clear that confusion, here is now my newest understanding. As I already wrote this in the classroom thread few days ago: The FTR is a structure that forms only AFTER a break of a level/zone. The FTR can become a FL when price bounces from it, hence the name (it limits the flag). The flag limit is just a property of the FTR. Report to moderator Quick Reply Reply Quote Thank You Jurij's Corner 12 Feb 2016 23:19 #44 MaxxAstral --> Offline Trader Posts: 17 Thank you received: 32 Jurij wrote: I have to correct my previous understanding of the FTR and FL. In one of the first post I wrote that for me a FL is a FTR of a previous FTR (something like an important FTR). Then I had a lot of trouble because of the markepedia FL page which shows FLs before a zone break (ie. FL without FTR). I would call those decision points rather than FLs. But now it is clear to me that there is no FL without FTR. And to clear that confusion, here is now my newest understanding. As I already wrote this in the classroom thread few days ago: The FTR is a structure that forms only AFTER a break of a level/zone. The FTR can become a FL when price bounces from it, hence the name (it limits the flag). The flag limit is just a property of the FTR. Here a chart from IF posted on FF Well yes a FL is the very extreme or the very Limit of a Flag beyond which price just can't go hence it kinda Limits the price beyond that. And basically all FLs are formed because of FTR, because price just can't return to the old price action zone thus again limiting price upto a certain level. That was an engulf where price DID move to the next FL, but that's all you can reasonably expect since you were on such a low time frame. I think the mistake was expecting price to KEEP going down on such a low time frame move. Usually I try to only use the M1 to validate a higher time frame move. I marked up your chart looking at it more holistically. 1. You see price engulfed what looks to be a fairly significant FL. And it engulfed it with a bull candle (2), which would suggest price wants to go up. At this point I would be looking for an area to enter a long trade. 3. Now price did engulf downward, but it was in the context of a larger move. Price was compressing into the bull candle. At the end of the compression, you would expect price to continue going up. Rather than go short here I would read price is just retracing before continuing its move up. 4. And you see the compression ended right at the s/r flip level, and price continued its move up. The s/r flip level and base of the pole are possible areas to look for a long entry, depending on your risk profile. When starting off, try to stick to the higher time frames for analysis. I bet if you were looking at the m5 or m15, it would have been easier to see that price wanted to move up. Attachments: Check this box to be notified of replies to this topic. Pred!ct0r Report to moderator Quick Reply Reply Quote Thank You Jurij's Corner 29 Mar 2016 00:48 #103 Jurij Topic Author --> Offline Associate Trader Think in terms of frequency Posts: 557 Thank you received: 1348 claudiuschan wrote: Jurij wrote: Psychology of stop hunting Hi Jurij, first of all thanks for the post, it really make me have more understanding on the market direction. Just a quick question, how you know which is the retailer stop? You know all retailers who follow trend put their stop below the last newly formed high/low in expectation for a trend continuation (new high/low). So retailer stops are just beyond pivot highs/lows, but here at RTM we know that the true orders are at the FTRs and those highs/lows are made sometimes to build traps so that ITs take the stops from retailers to get some extra liquidity. In that way, even if they are right on the direction, they lose. The idea with that chart is, once you know the new direction and target price wants to follow, when you see some highs or lows just above/below a fresh FTR then it is likely that price fakes out to the fresh zone. Report to moderator Quick Reply Reply Quote Thank You Jurij's Corner 08 Jun 2016 19:50 #206 Jurij Topic Author --> Offline Associate Trader Think in terms of frequency Posts: 557 Thank you received: 1348 Bodo, there is no right wrong. I understand your view. I saw the opportunity for a setup by looking on what flag limits/FTRs are important. For me your FTR3 is not important because it did not break anything on the left (on that scale). Price made a range (a box), meaning price flagged between two FTRs. Once price broke out to the upside from that range it made an FTR, a decision that price was to cheap below. Once this FTR breaks, the decision is made that price is no longer cheap and price is free to move to the other FTR which caused price to flag previously in that range (previous decision point that price was too cheap). The PAZ between those 2 FTRs This is how I draw the SPAZ Does it help to understand better my view? Personally for my own case, i won't know if price will come back down to your Stacked demand PAZ unless price was not able to engulf the supply but engulfed the FL2, which did happened later. Did i miss something important or my labels of DP were wrong? The stacked demand zone was not involved to see the trade opportunity because at that time the SPAZ wasn't there yet. Only the demand which is a reaction to your FTR3 made it a SPAZ. And there are no clues that price will go to the other end of the SPAZ until price engulfs the latest demand (tip of PAZ). Yes engulf of your FL2 is also a good opportunity. Attachments: Check this box to be notified of replies to this topic. Note: BBcode and smileys are still usable. Yes, which level is going to hold, the only trading question that matters. The journey for me to answer that question starts here and from the basics. So let's begin Disclaimer for this and all future posts: the following contents come from my own understanding of the original teachings by IF and other members, so always be aware that I could be totally wrong and that each unit of knowledge is subject to my own interpretation, filtering and may not reflect the original concepts as intended by IF Caps on price Every S/D trader knows them in and out, yet the best, strongest and perfect looking ones still fail. I can conclude from my own experience that the shape of the base and departure strength from a level have only limited influence on the overall outcome. What really matters, as RTM teaches, is the context. But before I get into that. There are some important clues that I consider to determine the quality of the base, I'm sure someone else here at RTM pointed them out. An interesting fact is that many traders think that consolidation (bases in RBD/RBD/RBR/DBD) means low activity (volume) and that momentum bars happen due to high volume. Sure, sometimes this is right, but most of the time momentum bars (liquidity gaps) are thin market moves (low volume) because price has to move in one direction once the last unfilled order is filled and ready to move to the next liquidity zone (base), where enough opposing orders get filled to stop price for some time, until again the balance gets broken one way or the other. This is also the reason why price bounces from those bases, because of unfilled orders left over from the last battle. S/D traders say that those orders at the bases are left there for undefined time, even for years. But it was a real revelation to me what RTM teaches about targets (PAZ). Another common reason for RBD/DBR failures is also explained by RTM. Just by knowing this and the above, we should be able to filter out many losses. Now to what really matters, the context where caps happen. Target 1 was there because of the past history: I see that in the last part I'm already ahead with FTRs, engulfs and targets. I will try to get in those in my next series of posts. And it is also clear from the above, that one concept taken in isolation (in this case price caps) is not enough to decipher price. Once this FTR breaks, the decision is made that price is no longer cheap and price is free to move to the other FTR which caused price to flag previously in that range (previous decision point that price was too cheap). The stacked demand zone was not involved to see the trade opportunity because at that time the SPAZ wasn't there yet. Only the demand which is a reaction to your FTR3 made it a SPAZ. And there are no clues that price will go to the other end of the SPAZ until price engulfs the latest demand (tip of PAZ). Yes engulf of your FL2 is also a good opportunity. ( price breaking into PAZ, by the truth, it breaks the last FTR before the PAZ, so simply enters the first one..., no breakings.. why we expect it will break all through ?.) That's because those are 2 different types of PAZs. Check out these two posts from Les_paul: post1 and post2 I think the SPAZ type works only if there is nothing important on the left, like a broken key level. Because the break of a key level makes it an FTR/FL. Also the reason for ITs creating stacked S/D is to pick up orders on the way and on return to fake out all classic S/D and S/R traders. Think about it this way, if ITs created those stacked demand/supply bases to fill their orders on the way, this means that on return there is little possibility of unfilled orders still left there. This is especially true for compression PAZs. That's why price needs to break only the last/first demand just before the CPAZ or SPAZ to make it through the entire zone. So if there are still unfilled orders then they are likely there at the tip (entrance of PAZ) and not inside that consumed zone. This is something that I think is the key to understand: 1. Some FL/FTRs work but many don't, so this concept is not enough on its own 2. Some engulfs work but many don't, so this concept is not enough on its own 3. PAZs (all types) work but many don't, so this concept is not enough on its own 4. QM/Diamond patterns work but many don't, so this concept is not enough on its own 5. Compression is sometimes a reversal sign but not always (LQ after compression is common) 6. S/D levels work but many don't 7. FO levels sometimes work but many don't ... I think it is clear where this is leading to. Perhaps this is exactly what IF means by saying that we need to make that final juxtaposition, where we see those concepts all at the same time. Often there is this common question in the homework section: "Why did that or this FTR/FL/CP/... fail?" Because it was never meant to work that way. Looking at the charts, there are almost dead sure setups that present itself only if multiple of the above RTM concepts appear together in the same setup. For example: at HTF supply, a trick is played (FO) then at the right shoulder of the trick level price forms an FTR/FL which happens to be a QM level also. Price meanwhile broke a lower FL and starts to retrace to the QM level. On approach price is starting to compress (making a CPAZ). Once price hits the QM FTR level at the FO key level at HTF supply price bounces and breaks into the CPAZ. If price now retraces back to the origin for a second chance entry then you have one of those almost dead sure trades Something like this past setup: Jurij wrote: CADJPY 30m Had a limit sell order not triggered, too high 5m LTF second chance (missed this one too) I think those setups are really nice and clear, that's what I want to trade more. I guess the difficulty in all this is to have the patience to wait and take only that kind of setups. Check this box to be notified of replies to this topic. Yes, which level is going to hold, the only trading question that matters. The journey for me to answer that question starts here and from the basics. So let's begin Disclaimer for this and all future posts: the following contents come from my own understanding of the original teachings by IF and other members, so always be aware that I could be totally wrong and that each unit of knowledge is subject to my own interpretation, filtering and may not reflect the original concepts as intended by IF Caps on price Every S/D trader knows them in and out, yet the best, strongest and perfect looking ones still fail. I can conclude from my own experience that the shape of the base and departure strength from a level have only limited influence on the overall outcome. What really matters, as RTM teaches, is the context. But before I get into that. There are some important clues that I consider to determine the quality of the base, I'm sure someone else here at RTM pointed them out. An interesting fact is that many traders think that consolidation (bases in RBD/RBD/RBR/DBD) means low activity (volume) and that momentum bars happen due to high volume. Sure, sometimes this is right, but most of the time momentum bars (liquidity gaps) are thin market moves (low volume) because price has to move in one direction once the last unfilled order is filled and ready to move to the next liquidity zone (base), where enough opposing orders get filled to stop price for some time, until again the balance gets broken one way or the other. This is also the reason why price bounces from those bases, because of unfilled orders left over from the last battle. S/D traders say that those orders at the bases are left there for undefined time, even for years. But it was a real revelation to me what RTM teaches about targets (PAZ). Another common reason for RBD/DBR failures is also explained by RTM. Just by knowing this and the above, we should be able to filter out many losses. Now to what really matters, the context where caps happen. Target 1 was there because of the past history: I see that in the last part I'm already ahead with FTRs, engulfs and targets. I will try to get in those in my next series of posts. And it is also clear from the above, that one concept taken in isolation (in this case price caps) is not enough to decipher price. I hope to be able to do this consistently Journal review: Jurij wrote: NZDCAD DM in play? 4H 30m initial QM spotted by a trading mate, so not all my credit Looking back at this, at that time it was a solid looking setup to me. The problem and the error I've been doing is to consider scales, making everything more complicated than it is, especially mixing smaller and higher scale FTR/FL boxes. But the market doesn't care about boxes with fixed rules (for ex. 4H box is stronger than 5m box and an eng is a signal...). If a 4H FTR/FL box is made as a reaction to a 1m FL it is because of these orders sitting there. Orders have not time frames because they are just orders. There are levels that are stronger than others, not because of time frame but because of orders and decisions of greater or lesser importance (swap levels vs simple barriers...) Thanks to Salivan and Omid I began to focus on the real orders (true supply/demand aka FL) and this was a big missing piece in my analysis Attachments: Check this box to be notified of replies to this topic. "...But FOF is only present with PA, until then it is just unfilled orders that could bounce price " many thanks all the best Salivan explained nicely FOF in his jorunal. Basically unfilled orders are one thing but FOF is different. For example if we have unfilled orders we can expect only a bounce. If we have PA (signal/intention) then the last set of unfilled orders becomes FOF as there are no orders beyond that FOF level. Without the signal, we have just the last set of unfilled orders but no guarantee that the level holds. If the ITs filled all their orders beyond a certain level, it doesn't make sense to fake out past it, they must hate drawdown too... That last level will have all limit orders of the ITs to make sure it doesn't break. Once tg is hit, those orders are removed. And price is allowed to break that level. That's my understanding of FOF as of now and since I'm new to FOF as well, I'm not really sure about it yet. Hope it helps. Check this box to be notified of replies to this topic. First the charts As you can see price stopped at the first opposing FL of that scale (good for 1st profit tg). Then the pivot low 30m FL base, was not a good point for the full reversal. Reasons: 1. the base was a pivot low, which means a reaction to a previous base, in this case a 30m FTR (which itself is the top of a small CP) 2. the sharp arrival and departure makes this more a stop hunt/fake out than a full reversal, also because most reversals have larger tops with QM/diamond levels 3.this low (where my entry was) and the pivot low can be used by ITs for future tricks (FO), whereas that small 30m FTR looks absolutely not interesting to retail traders 4. the better entry can be seen on chart #2 after the new 1m engulf signal either at the 1m quasimodo level or at the origin of the engulf, with the stop below the ftr base, I started to doubt about the validity of that engulf, but in the end price reached the target FL above. The question remains as how far price can retrace before meeting it's original target after an engulf Attachments: Check this box to be notified of replies to this topic. READ: Analysis paralysis. Price is bouncing from fresh H4 supply (you marked it correctly, well done) to next H4 demand. Then Price does what it does 24 a day 5 days a week.... f#€% with traders. So... Price moves, hits supply, forms a DP, DP breaks the HLs sequence and we get LL. Hence DP is confirmed and we are good to trade this thing lower. Then price reacts to FL... makes a bounce (money to be made there as well). It is not enough then price moves higher to test the DP... does not reach it at 1st attempt. Poor fellows short it.. put stops above. Then Big fellows decide it is great place to get filled. They push it up.. hunt stops.. hit DP. Then this thing moves lower. All this drama happens in the big picture: From H4 supply to H4 demand (or lower... haven't checked). So basically you were buying where everyone was selling. Now you know. Promise you will not do it again, make a poster, a mantra etc. Focus on the next setup and don't let last loss to mess with you since it has nothing to do with the next setup. Have a great evening. In one of the first post I wrote that for me a FL is a FTR of a previous FTR (something like an important FTR). Then I had a lot of trouble because of the markepedia FL page which shows FLs before a zone break (ie. FL without FTR). I would call those decision points rather than FLs. But now it is clear to me that there is no FL without FTR. And to clear that confusion, here is now my newest understanding. As I already wrote this in the classroom thread few days ago: The FTR is a structure that forms only AFTER a break of a level/zone. The FTR can become a FL when price bounces from it, hence the name (it limits the flag). The flag limit is just a property of the FTR. In one of the first post I wrote that for me a FL is a FTR of a previous FTR (something like an important FTR). Then I had a lot of trouble because of the markepedia FL page which shows FLs before a zone break (ie. FL without FTR). I would call those decision points rather than FLs. But now it is clear to me that there is no FL without FTR. And to clear that confusion, here is now my newest understanding. As I already wrote this in the classroom thread few days ago: The FTR is a structure that forms only AFTER a break of a level/zone. The FTR can become a FL when price bounces from it, hence the name (it limits the flag). The flag limit is just a property of the FTR. Here a chart from IF posted on FF Well yes a FL is the very extreme or the very Limit of a Flag beyond which price just can't go hence it kinda Limits the price beyond that. And basically all FLs are formed because of FTR, because price just can't return to the old price action zone thus again limiting price upto a certain level. But thanks for bringing up this crucial concept for clarification of all in here, and also for referring to that diagram by IF. It says all. Check this box to be notified of replies to this topic. That was an engulf where price DID move to the next FL, but that's all you can reasonably expect since you were on such a low time frame. I think the mistake was expecting price to KEEP going down on such a low time frame move. Usually I try to only use the M1 to validate a higher time frame move. I marked up your chart looking at it more holistically. 1. You see price engulfed what looks to be a fairly significant FL. And it engulfed it with a bull candle (2), which would suggest price wants to go up. At this point I would be looking for an area to enter a long trade. 3. Now price did engulf downward, but it was in the context of a larger move. Price was compressing into the bull candle. At the end of the compression, you would expect price to continue going up. Rather than go short here I would read price is just retracing before continuing its move up. 4. And you see the compression ended right at the s/r flip level, and price continued its move up. The s/r flip level and base of the pole are possible areas to look for a long entry, depending on your risk profile. When starting off, try to stick to the higher time frames for analysis. I bet if you were looking at the m5 or m15, it would have been easier to see that price wanted to move up. Attachments: Check this box to be notified of replies to this topic. Pred!ct0r Report to moderator Quick Reply Reply Quote Thank You Jurij's Corner 29 Mar 2016 00:48 #103 Jurij Topic Author --> Offline Associate Trader Think in terms of frequency Posts: 557 Thank you received: 1348 claudiuschan wrote: Jurij wrote: Psychology of stop hunting Hi Jurij, first of all thanks for the post, it really make me have more understanding on the market direction. Just a quick question, how you know which is the retailer stop? You know all retailers who follow trend put their stop below the last newly formed high/low in expectation for a trend continuation (new high/low). So retailer stops are just beyond pivot highs/lows, but here at RTM we know that the true orders are at the FTRs and those highs/lows are made sometimes to build traps so that ITs take the stops from retailers to get some extra liquidity. In that way, even if they are right on the direction, they lose. The idea with that chart is, once you know the new direction and target price wants to follow, when you see some highs or lows just above/below a fresh FTR then it is likely that price fakes out to the fresh zone. There are some important clues that I consider to determine the quality of the base, I'm sure someone else here at RTM pointed them out. https://www.readthemarket.com/index.php/en/forum/journals/2410-jurij-s-corner 5/58 7/27/2018 Jurij's Corner - RTM Community HOME EDUCATION FORUM MORE LOGOUT An interesting fact is that many traders think that consolidation (bases in RBD/RBD/RBR/DBD) means low activity (volume) and that momentum bars happen due to high volume. Sure, sometimes this is right, but most of the time momentum bars (liquidity gaps) are thin market moves (low volume) because price has to move in one direction once the last unfilled order is filled and ready to move to the next liquidity zone https://www.readthemarket.com/index.php/en/forum/journals/2410-jurij-s-corner 6/58 7/27/2018 Jurij's Corner - RTM Community (base), where enough opposing orders get filled to stop price for some time, until again HOME EDUCATION FORUM MORE LOGOUT the balance gets broken one way or the other. This is also the reason why price bounces from those bases, because of unfilled orders left over from the last battle. S/D traders say that those orders at the bases are left there for undefined time, even for years. But it was a real revelation to me what RTM teaches about targets (PAZ). Another common reason for RBD/DBR failures is also explained by RTM. https://www.readthemarket.com/index.php/en/forum/journals/2410-jurij-s-corner 7/58 7/27/2018 Jurij's Corner - RTM Community HOME EDUCATION FORUM MORE LOGOUT Just by knowing this and the above, we should be able to filter out many losses. Check out these two posts from Les_paul: post1 and post2 I think the SPAZ type works only if there is nothing important on the left, like a broken key level. Because the break of a key level makes it an FTR/FL. Also the reason for ITs creating stacked S/D is to pick up orders on the way and on return to fake out all classic S/D and S/R traders. Think about it this way, if ITs created those stacked demand/supply bases to fill their orders on the way, this means that on return there is little possibility of unfilled orders still left there. This is especially true for compression PAZs. That's why price needs to break only the last/first demand just before the CPAZ or SPAZ to make it through the entire zone. So if there are still unfilled orders then they are likely there at the tip (entrance of PAZ) and not inside that consumed zone. S/D levels work but many don't 7. FO levels sometimes work but many don't ... I think it is clear where this is leading to. Perhaps this is exactly what IF means by saying that we need to make that final juxtaposition, where we see those concepts all at the same time. Often there is this common question in the homework section: "Why did that or this FTR/FL/CP/... fail?" Because it was never meant to work that way. Looking at the charts, there are almost dead sure setups that present itself only if multiple of the above RTM concepts appear together in the same setup. For example: at HTF supply, a trick is played (FO) then at the right shoulder of the trick level price forms an FTR/FL which happens to be a QM level also. Price meanwhile broke a lower FL and starts to retrace to the QM level. On approach price is starting to compress (making a CPAZ). Once price hits the QM FTR level at the FO key level at HTF supply price bounces and breaks into the CPAZ. If price now retraces back to the origin for a second chance entry then you have one of those almost dead sure trades Something like this past setup: Jurij wrote: CADJPY 30m Had a limit sell order not triggered, too high https://www.readthemarket.com/index.php/en/forum/journals/2410-jurij-s-corner?start=225 15/53 7/27/2018 Jurij's Corner - Page 10 - RTM Community HOME EDUCATION FORUM MORE LOGOUT 5m LTF second chance (missed this one too) I think those setups are really nice and clear, that's what I want to trade more. Hi Jurij, I have been working on the same Question. I tried only trading in the direction of the HTF scale Engulf but when this is 4 hour or higher the best trades are on a deep retrace of the HTF Engulf at least for R:R. Having said that trading the LTF scale engulf in the opposite direction of the HTF engulf produces good trades. With patience I guess waiting on the deep retrace of the HTF scale engulf is best but you also miss so many trades. I find by taking what the market has to offer on LTF Scale one can more than cover the cost of getting the HTF Scale wrong, when it appears we have retraced enough ie nearing the extreme of this scale I wait and play the HTF Scale again in the direction of the HTF engulf. The problem and the error I've been doing is to consider scales, making everything more complicated than it is, especially mixing smaller and higher scale FTR/FL boxes. But the market doesn't care about boxes with fixed rules (for ex. 4H box is stronger than 5m box and an eng is a signal...). If a 4H FTR/FL box is made as a reaction to a 1m FL it is because of these orders sitting there. Orders have not time frames because they are just orders. There are levels that are stronger than others, not because of time frame but because of orders and decisions of greater or lesser importance (swap levels vs simple barriers...) First the charts https://www.readthemarket.com/index.php/en/forum/journals/2410-jurij-s-corner?start=25 2/54 7/27/2018 Jurij's Corner - Page 2 - RTM Community HOME EDUCATION FORUM MORE LOGOUT As you can see price stopped at the first opposing FL of that scale (good for 1st profit tg). Then the pivot low 30m FL base, was not a good point for the full reversal. Reasons: 1. the base was a pivot low, which means a reaction to a previous base, in this case a 30m FTR (which itself is the top of a small CP) 2. the sharp arrival and departure makes this more a stop hunt/fake out than a full reversal, also because most reversals have larger tops with QM/diamond levels 3.this low (where my entry was) and the pivot low can be used by ITs for future tricks (FO), whereas that small 30m FTR looks absolutely not interesting to retail traders 4. the better entry can be seen on chart #2 after the new 1m engulf signal either at the 1m quasimodo level or at the origin of the engulf, with the stop below the ftr base, I started to doubt about the validity of that engulf, but in the end price reached the target FL above. In one of the first post I wrote that for me a FL is a FTR of a previous FTR (something like an important FTR). Then I had a lot of trouble because of the markepedia FL page which shows FLs before a zone break (ie. FL without FTR). I would call those decision points rather than FLs. But now it is clear to me that there is no FL without FTR. And to clear that confusion, here is now my newest understanding. As I already wrote this in the classroom thread few days ago: The FTR is a structure that forms only AFTER a break of a level/zone. The FTR can become a FL when price bounces from it, hence the name (it limits the flag). The flag limit is just a property of the FTR. https://www.readthemarket.com/index.php/en/forum/journals/2410-jurij-s-corner?start=25 34/54 7/27/2018 Jurij's Corner - Page 2 - RTM Community Here a drawing from IF posted on FF HOME EDUCATION FORUM MORE LOGOUT Attachments: The following user(s) said Thank You: MaxxAstral, cuimingzhao "And those who were seen dancing were thought to be insane by those who could not hear the music." Then I had a lot of trouble because of the markepedia FL page which shows FLs before a zone break (ie. FL without FTR). I would call those decision points rather than FLs. But now it is clear to me that there is no FL without FTR. And to clear that confusion, here is now my newest understanding. As I already wrote this in the classroom thread few days ago: The FTR is a structure that forms only AFTER a break of a level/zone. The FTR can become a FL when price bounces from it, hence the name (it limits the flag). The flag limit is just a property of the FTR. Here a chart from IF posted on FF https://www.readthemarket.com/index.php/en/forum/journals/2410-jurij-s-corner?start=25 36/54 7/27/2018 Jurij's Corner - Page 2 - RTM Community HOME EDUCATION FORUM MORE LOGOUT Well yes a FL is the very extreme or the very Limit of a Flag beyond which price just can't go hence it kinda Limits the price beyond that. And basically all FLs are formed because of FTR, because price just can't return to the old price action zone thus again limiting price upto a certain level. But thanks for bringing up this crucial concept for clarification of all in here, and also for referring to that diagram by IF. It says all. "...But FOF is only present with PA, until then it is just unfilled orders that could bounce price " many thanks all the best Salivan explained nicely FOF in his jorunal. Basically unfilled orders are one thing but FOF is different. For example if we have unfilled orders we can expect only a bounce. If we have PA (signal/intention) then the last set of unfilled orders becomes FOF as there are no orders beyond that FOF level. Without the signal, we have just the last set of unfilled orders but no guarantee that the level holds. If the ITs filled all their orders beyond a certain level, it doesn't make sense to fake out past it, they must hate drawdown too... That last level will have all limit orders of the ITs to make sure it doesn't break. Once tg is hit, those orders are removed. And price is allowed to break that level. That's my understanding of FOF as of now and since I'm new to FOF as well, I'm not really sure about it yet. Hope it helps. Friedrich Nietzsche QUICK REPLY REPLY QUOTE THANK YOU Jurij's Corner #52 ahdat Offline Trader Posts: 102 Thank you received: 125 Hey Jurij, wanted to give my take on what happened to your trade. That was an engulf where price DID move to the next FL, but that's all you can reasonably expect since you were on such a low time frame. I think the mistake was expecting price to KEEP going down on such a low time frame move. Usually I try to only use the M1 to validate a higher time frame move. I marked up your chart looking at it more holistically. 1. You see price engulfed what looks to be a fairly significant FL. And it engulfed it with https://www.readthemarket.com/index.php/en/forum/journals/2410-jurij-s-corner?start=50 3/41 7/27/2018 Jurij's Corner - Page 3 - RTM Community a bull candle (2), which would suggest price wants to go up. At this point I would be HOME EDUCATION FORUM MORE LOGOUT looking for an area to enter a long trade. 3. Now price did engulf downward, but it was in the context of a larger move. Price was compressing into the bull candle. At the end of the compression, you would expect price to continue going up. Rather than go short here I would read price is just retracing before continuing its move up. 4. And you see the compression ended right at the s/r flip level, and price continued its move up. The s/r flip level and base of the pole are possible areas to look for a long entry, depending on your risk profile. When starting off, try to stick to the higher time frames for analysis. I bet if you were looking at the m5 or m15, it would have been easier to see that price wanted to move up. LOGOUT HOME EDUCATION FORUM MORE Just a quick question, how you know which is the retailer stop? You know all retailers who follow trend put their stop below the last newly formed high/low in expectation for a trend continuation (new high/low). So retailer stops are just beyond pivot highs/lows, but here at RTM we know that the true orders are at the FTRs and those highs/lows are made sometimes to build traps so that ITs take the stops from retailers to get some extra liquidity. In that way, even if they are right on the direction, they lose. The idea with that chart is, once you know the new direction and target price wants to follow, when you see some highs or lows just above/below a fresh FTR then it is likely that price fakes out to the fresh zone. Yes, which level is going to hold, the only trading question that matters. The journey for me to answer that question starts here and from the basics. So let's begin Disclaimer for this and all future posts: the following contents come from my own understanding of the original teachings by IF and other members, so always be aware that I could be totally wrong and that each unit of knowledge is subject to my own interpretation, filtering and may not reflect the original concepts as intended by IF Caps on price Every S/D trader knows them in and out, yet the best, strongest and perfect looking ones still fail. I can conclude from my own experience that the shape of the base and departure strength from a level have only limited influence on the overall outcome. What really matters, as RTM teaches, is the context. But before I get into that. There are some important clues that I consider to determine the quality of the base, I'm sure someone else here at RTM pointed them out. An interesting fact is that many traders think that consolidation (bases in RBD/RBD/RBR/DBD) means low activity (volume) and that momentum bars happen due to high volume. Sure, sometimes this is right, but most of the time momentum bars (liquidity gaps) are thin market moves (low volume) because price has to move in one direction once the last unfilled order is filled and ready to move to the next liquidity zone (base), where enough opposing orders get filled to stop price for some time, until again the balance gets broken one way or the other. This is also the reason why price bounces from those bases, because of unfilled orders left over from the last battle. S/D traders say that those orders at the bases are left there for undefined time, even for years. But it was a real revelation to me what RTM teaches about targets (PAZ). Another common reason for RBD/DBR failures is also explained by RTM. Just by knowing this and the above, we should be able to filter out many losses. Now to what really matters, the context where caps happen. Target 1 was there because of the past history: I see that in the last part I'm already ahead with FTRs, engulfs and targets. I will try to get in those in my next series of posts. And it is also clear from the above, that one concept taken in isolation (in this case price caps) is not enough to decipher price. ( price breaking into PAZ, by the truth, it breaks the last FTR before the PAZ, so simply enters the first one..., no breakings.. why we expect it will break all through ?.) That's because those are 2 different types of PAZs. Check out these two posts from Les_paul: post1 and post2 I think the SPAZ type works only if there is nothing important on the left, like a broken key level. Because the break of a key level makes it an FTR/FL. Also the reason for ITs creating stacked S/D is to pick up orders on the way and on return to fake out all classic S/D and S/R traders. Think about it this way, if ITs created those stacked demand/supply bases to fill their orders on the way, this means that on return there is little possibility of unfilled orders still left there. This is especially true for compression PAZs. That's why price needs to break only the last/first demand just before the CPAZ or SPAZ to make it through the entire zone. So if there are still unfilled orders then they are likely there at the tip (entrance of PAZ) and not inside that consumed zone. Report to moderator Quick Reply Reply Quote Thank You Jurij's Corner 12 Jun 2016 17:54 #232 Jurij Topic Author --> Offline Associate Trader Think in terms of frequency Posts: 557 Thank you received: 1348 althoufx wrote: [...] ......yes Jurji i remember those posts, also because LP said later to be not enough confident on this stuff for keeping trades based on this knowledge, then it looked like a topic not yet solved, as in stand-by conditions. So those posts were instead taken as pieces of the puzzle...am i wrong ? thanks for your reply !! Right, PAZs are just a piece of the puzzle like everything else. This is something that I think is the key to understand: 1. Some FL/FTRs work but many don't, so this concept is not enough on its own 2. Some engulfs work but many don't, so this concept is not enough on its own 3. PAZs (all types) work but many don't, so this concept is not enough on its own 4. QM/Diamond patterns work but many don't, so this concept is not enough on its own 5. Compression is sometimes a reversal sign but not always (LQ after compression is common) 6. S/D levels work but many don't 7. FO levels sometimes work but many don't ... I think it is clear where this is leading to. Perhaps this is exactly what IF means by saying that we need to make that final juxtaposition, where we see those concepts all at the same time. Often there is this common question in the homework section: "Why did that or this FTR/FL/CP/... fail?" Because it was never meant to work that way. Looking at the charts, there are almost dead sure setups that present itself only if multiple of the above RTM concepts appear together in the same setup. For example: at HTF supply, a trick is played (FO) then at the right shoulder of the trick level price forms an FTR/FL which happens to be a QM level also. Price meanwhile broke a lower FL and starts to retrace to the QM level. On approach price is starting to compress (making a CPAZ). Once price hits the QM FTR level at the FO key level at HTF supply price bounces and breaks into the CPAZ. If price now retraces back to the origin for a second chance entry then you have one of those almost dead sure trades Something like this past setup: Jurij wrote: CADJPY 30m Had a limit sell order not triggered, too high 5m LTF second chance (missed this one too) I think those setups are really nice and clear, that's what I want to trade more. I guess the difficulty in all this is to have the patience to wait and take only that kind of setups. Check this box to be notified of replies to this topic. First the charts As you can see price stopped at the first opposing FL of that scale (good for 1st profit tg). Then the pivot low 30m FL base, was not a good point for the full reversal. Reasons: 1. the base was a pivot low, which means a reaction to a previous base, in this case a 30m FTR (which itself is the top of a small CP) 2. the sharp arrival and departure makes this more a stop hunt/fake out than a full reversal, also because most reversals have larger tops with QM/diamond levels 3.this low (where my entry was) and the pivot low can be used by ITs for future tricks (FO), whereas that small 30m FTR looks absolutely not interesting to retail traders 4. the better entry can be seen on chart #2 after the new 1m engulf signal either at the 1m quasimodo level or at the origin of the engulf, with the stop below the ftr base, I started to doubt about the validity of that engulf, but in the end price reached the target FL above. The question remains as how far price can retrace before meeting it's original target after an engulf Attachments: Check this box to be notified of replies to this topic. The good thing is that I drew in the 5m FL base where the play happened before price reached it. I take away the following simple lesson for today: It is really important to always draw FLs/FTRs (one above and one below) ahead of price in each different scale (TF), because when the tricks happen you can spot them in real time and act accordingly. READ: Analysis paralysis. Price is bouncing from fresh H4 supply (you marked it correctly, well done) to next H4 demand. Then Price does what it does 24 a day 5 days a week.... f#€% with traders. So... Price moves, hits supply, forms a DP, DP breaks the HLs sequence and we get LL. Hence DP is confirmed and we are good to trade this thing lower. Then price reacts to FL... makes a bounce (money to be made there as well). It is not enough then price moves higher to test the DP... does not reach it at 1st attempt. Poor fellows short it.. put stops above. Then Big fellows decide it is great place to get filled. They push it up.. hunt stops.. hit DP. Then this thing moves lower. All this drama happens in the big picture: From H4 supply to H4 demand (or lower... haven't checked). So basically you were buying where everyone was selling. Now you know. Promise you will not do it again, make a poster, a mantra etc. Focus on the next setup and don't let last loss to mess with you since it has nothing to do with the next setup. Have a great evening. Art. Attachments: Check this box to be notified of replies to this topic. Note: BBcode and smileys are still usable. Report to moderator Quick Reply Reply Quote Thank You Jurij's Corner 12 Feb 2016 23:07 #43 Jurij Topic Author --> Offline Associate Trader Think in terms of frequency Posts: 557 Thank you received: 1348 I have to correct my previous understanding of the FTR and FL. In one of the first post I wrote that for me a FL is a FTR of a previous FTR (something like an important FTR). Then I had a lot of trouble because of the markepedia FL page which shows FLs before a zone break (ie. FL without FTR). I would call those decision points rather than FLs. But now it is clear to me that there is no FL without FTR. And to clear that confusion, here is now my newest understanding. As I already wrote this in the classroom thread few days ago: The FTR is a structure that forms only AFTER a break of a level/zone. The FTR can become a FL when price bounces from it, hence the name (it limits the flag). The flag limit is just a property of the FTR. Here a drawing from IF posted on FF Attachments: Check this box to be notified of replies to this topic. Note: BBcode and smileys are still usable. Report to moderator Quick Reply Reply Quote Thank You Jurij's Corner 12 Feb 2016 23:19 #44 MaxxAstral --> Offline Trader Posts: 17 Thank you received: 32 Jurij wrote: I have to correct my previous understanding of the FTR and FL. In one of the first post I wrote that for me a FL is a FTR of a previous FTR (something like an important FTR). Then I had a lot of trouble because of the markepedia FL page which shows FLs before a zone break (ie. FL without FTR). I would call those decision points rather than FLs. But now it is clear to me that there is no FL without FTR. And to clear that confusion, here is now my newest understanding. As I already wrote this in the classroom thread few days ago: The FTR is a structure that forms only AFTER a break of a level/zone. The FTR can become a FL when price bounces from it, hence the name (it limits the flag). The flag limit is just a property of the FTR. Here a chart from IF posted on FF Well yes a FL is the very extreme or the very Limit of a Flag beyond which price just can't go hence it kinda Limits the price beyond that. And basically all FLs are formed because of FTR, because price just can't return to the old price action zone thus again limiting price upto a certain level. But thanks for bringing up this crucial concept for clarification of all in here, and also for referring to that diagram by IF. It says all. Check this box to be notified of replies to this topic. The following user(s) said Thank You: cuimingzhao “And those who were seen dancing were thought to be insane by those who could not hear the music.” ― Friedrich Nietzsche Report to moderator Quick Reply Reply Quote Thank You Jurij's Corner 19 Feb 2016 15:38 #52 ahdat --> Offline Trader Posts: 102 Thank you received: 125 Hey Jurij, wanted to give my take on what happened to your trade. That was an engulf where price DID move to the next FL, but that's all you can reasonably expect since you were on such a low time frame. I think the mistake was expecting price to KEEP going down on such a low time frame move. Usually I try to only use the M1 to validate a higher time frame move. I marked up your chart looking at it more holistically. 1. You see price engulfed what looks to be a fairly significant FL. And it engulfed it with a bull candle (2), which would suggest price wants to go up. At this point I would be looking for an area to enter a long trade. 3. Now price did engulf downward, but it was in the context of a larger move. Price was compressing into the bull candle. At the end of the compression, you would expect price to continue going up. Rather than go short here I would read price is just retracing before continuing its move up. 4. And you see the compression ended right at the s/r flip level, and price continued its move up. The s/r flip level and base of the pole are possible areas to look for a long entry, depending on your risk profile. When starting off, try to stick to the higher time frames for analysis. I bet if you were looking at the m5 or m15, it would have been easier to see that price wanted to move up. Attachments: Check this box to be notified of replies to this topic. Pred!ct0r Report to moderator Quick Reply Reply Quote Thank You Jurij's Corner 29 Mar 2016 00:48 #103 Jurij Topic Author --> Offline Associate Trader Think in terms of frequency Posts: 557 Thank you received: 1348 claudiuschan wrote: Jurij wrote: Psychology of stop hunting Hi Jurij, first of all thanks for the post, it really make me have more understanding on the market direction. Just a quick question, how you know which is the retailer stop? You know all retailers who follow trend put their stop below the last newly formed high/low in expectation for a trend continuation (new high/low). So retailer stops are just beyond pivot highs/lows, but here at RTM we know that the true orders are at the FTRs and those highs/lows are made sometimes to build traps so that ITs take the stops from retailers to get some extra liquidity. In that way, even if they are right on the direction, they lose. The idea with that chart is, once you know the new direction and target price wants to follow, when you see some highs or lows just above/below a fresh FTR then it is likely that price fakes out to the fresh zone. Report to moderator Quick Reply Reply Quote Thank You Jurij's Corner 08 Jun 2016 19:50 #206 Jurij Topic Author --> Offline Associate Trader Think in terms of frequency Posts: 557 Thank you received: 1348 Bodo, there is no right wrong. I understand your view. I saw the opportunity for a setup by looking on what flag limits/FTRs are important. For me your FTR3 is not important because it did not break anything on the left (on that scale). Price made a range (a box), meaning price flagged between two FTRs. Once price broke out to the upside from that range it made an FTR, a decision that price was to cheap below. Once this FTR breaks, the decision is made that price is no longer cheap and price is free to move to the other FTR which caused price to flag previously in that range (previous decision point that price was too cheap). The PAZ between those 2 FTRs This is how I draw the SPAZ Does it help to understand better my view? Personally for my own case, i won't know if price will come back down to your Stacked demand PAZ unless price was not able to engulf the supply but engulfed the FL2, which did happened later. Did i miss something important or my labels of DP were wrong? The stacked demand zone was not involved to see the trade opportunity because at that time the SPAZ wasn't there yet. Only the demand which is a reaction to your FTR3 made it a SPAZ. And there are no clues that price will go to the other end of the SPAZ until price engulfs the latest demand (tip of PAZ). Yes engulf of your FL2 is also a good opportunity. Attachments: Check this box to be notified of replies to this topic. Note: BBcode and smileys are still usable. I saw the opportunity for a setup by looking on what flag limits/FTRs are important. For me your FTR3 is not important because it did not break anything on the left (on that scale). Price made a range (a box), meaning price flagged between two FTRs. Once price broke out to the upside from that range it made an FTR, a decision that price was to cheap below. Once this FTR breaks, the decision is made that price is no longer cheap and price is free to move to the other FTR which caused price to flag previously in that range (previous decision point that price was too cheap). The stacked demand zone was not involved to see the trade opportunity because at that time the SPAZ wasn't there yet. Only the demand which is a reaction to your FTR3 made it a SPAZ. And there are no clues that price will go to the other end of the SPAZ until price engulfs the latest demand (tip of PAZ). Yes engulf of your FL2 is also a good opportunity. The following user(s) said Thank You: naascott , Jurij , erfada , pardis , alirezat , cuimingzhao With time, patience and experience, what once seemed very complex becomes very simple indeed Please join www.theblue.community Report to moderator Quick Reply Reply Quote Thank You Jurij's Corner 09 Jan 2016 21:46 #3 Jurij Topic Author --> Offline Associate Trader Think in terms of frequency Posts: 557 Thank you received: 1348 Thanks IF. Yes, which level is going to hold, the only trading question that matters. The journey for me to answer that question starts here and from the basics. So let's begin Disclaimer for this and all future posts: the following contents come from my own understanding of the original teachings by IF and other members, so always be aware that I could be totally wrong and that each unit of knowledge is subject to my own interpretation, filtering and may not reflect the original concepts as intended by IF Caps on price Every S/D trader knows them in and out, yet the best, strongest and perfect looking ones still fail. I can conclude from my own experience that the shape of the base and departure strength from a level have only limited influence on the overall outcome. What really matters, as RTM teaches, is the context. But before I get into that. There are some important clues that I consider to determine the quality of the base, I'm sure someone else here at RTM pointed them out. An interesting fact is that many traders think that consolidation (bases in RBD/RBD/RBR/DBD) means low activity (volume) and that momentum bars happen due to high volume. Sure, sometimes this is right, but most of the time momentum bars (liquidity gaps) are thin market moves (low volume) because price has to move in one direction once the last unfilled order is filled and ready to move to the next liquidity zone (base), where enough opposing orders get filled to stop price for some time, until again the balance gets broken one way or the other. This is also the reason why price bounces from those bases, because of unfilled orders left over from the last battle. S/D traders say that those orders at the bases are left there for undefined time, even for years. But it was a real revelation to me what RTM teaches about targets (PAZ). Another common reason for RBD/DBR failures is also explained by RTM. Just by knowing this and the above, we should be able to filter out many losses. Now to what really matters, the context where caps happen. Target 1 was there because of the past history: I see that in the last part I'm already ahead with FTRs, engulfs and targets. I will try to get in those in my next series of posts. And it is also clear from the above, that one concept taken in isolation (in this case price caps) is not enough to decipher price. I understand your view. I saw the opportunity for a setup by looking on what flag limits/FTRs are important. For me your FTR3 is not important because it did not break anything on the left (on that scale). Price made a range (a box), meaning price flagged between two FTRs. Once price broke out to the upside from that range it made an FTR, a decision that price was to cheap below. Once this FTR breaks, the decision is made that price is no longer cheap and price is free to move to the other FTR which caused price to flag previously in that range (previous decision point that price was too cheap). The PAZ between those 2 FTRs This is how I draw the SPAZ Does it help to understand better my view? Personally for my own case, i won't know if price will come back down to your Stacked demand PAZ unless price was not able to engulf the supply but engulfed the FL2, which did happened later. Did i miss something important or my labels of DP were wrong? The stacked demand zone was not involved to see the trade opportunity because at that time the SPAZ wasn't there yet. Only the demand which is a reaction to your FTR3 made it a SPAZ. And there are no clues that price will go to the other end of the SPAZ until price engulfs the latest demand (tip of PAZ). Yes engulf of your FL2 is also a good opportunity. Attachments: Check this box to be notified of replies to this topic. Note: BBcode and smileys are still usable. ( price breaking into PAZ, by the truth, it breaks the last FTR before the PAZ, so simply enters the first one..., no breakings.. why we expect it will break all through ?.) That's because those are 2 different types of PAZs. Check out these two posts from Les_paul: post1 and post2 I think the SPAZ type works only if there is nothing important on the left, like a broken key level. Because the break of a key level makes it an FTR/FL. Also the reason for ITs creating stacked S/D is to pick up orders on the way and on return to fake out all classic S/D and S/R traders. Think about it this way, if ITs created those stacked demand/supply bases to fill their orders on the way, this means that on return there is little possibility of unfilled orders still left there. This is especially true for compression PAZs. That's why price needs to break only the last/first demand just before the CPAZ or SPAZ to make it through the entire zone. So if there are still unfilled orders then they are likely there at the tip (entrance of PAZ) and not inside that consumed zone. Report to moderator Quick Reply Reply Quote Thank You Jurij's Corner 12 Jun 2016 17:54 #232 Jurij Topic Author --> Offline Associate Trader Think in terms of frequency Posts: 557 Thank you received: 1348 althoufx wrote: [...] ......yes Jurji i remember those posts, also because LP said later to be not enough confident on this stuff for keeping trades based on this knowledge, then it looked like a topic not yet solved, as in stand-by conditions. So those posts were instead taken as pieces of the puzzle...am i wrong ? thanks for your reply !! Right, PAZs are just a piece of the puzzle like everything else. This is something that I think is the key to understand: 1. Some FL/FTRs work but many don't, so this concept is not enough on its own 2. Some engulfs work but many don't, so this concept is not enough on its own 3. PAZs (all types) work but many don't, so this concept is not enough on its own 4. QM/Diamond patterns work but many don't, so this concept is not enough on its own 5. Compression is sometimes a reversal sign but not always (LQ after compression is common) 6. S/D levels work but many don't 7. FO levels sometimes work but many don't ... I think it is clear where this is leading to. Perhaps this is exactly what IF means by saying that we need to make that final juxtaposition, where we see those concepts all at the same time. Often there is this common question in the homework section: "Why did that or this FTR/FL/CP/... fail?" Because it was never meant to work that way. Looking at the charts, there are almost dead sure setups that present itself only if multiple of the above RTM concepts appear together in the same setup. For example: at HTF supply, a trick is played (FO) then at the right shoulder of the trick level price forms an FTR/FL which happens to be a QM level also. Price meanwhile broke a lower FL and starts to retrace to the QM level. On approach price is starting to compress (making a CPAZ). Once price hits the QM FTR level at the FO key level at HTF supply price bounces and breaks into the CPAZ. If price now retraces back to the origin for a second chance entry then you have one of those almost dead sure trades Something like this past setup: Jurij wrote: CADJPY 30m Had a limit sell order not triggered, too high 5m LTF second chance (missed this one too) I think those setups are really nice and clear, that's what I want to trade more. I guess the difficulty in all this is to have the patience to wait and take only that kind of setups. Check this box to be notified of replies to this topic. Yes, which level is going to hold, the only trading question that matters. The journey for me to answer that question starts here and from the basics. So let's begin Disclaimer for this and all future posts: the following contents come from my own understanding of the original teachings by IF and other members, so always be aware that I could be totally wrong and that each unit of knowledge is subject to my own interpretation, filtering and may not reflect the original concepts as intended by IF Caps on price Every S/D trader knows them in and out, yet the best, strongest and perfect looking ones still fail. I can conclude from my own experience that the shape of the base and departure strength from a level have only limited influence on the overall outcome. What really matters, as RTM teaches, is the context. But before I get into that. There are some important clues that I consider to determine the quality of the base, I'm sure someone else here at RTM pointed them out. An interesting fact is that many traders think that consolidation (bases in RBD/RBD/RBR/DBD) means low activity (volume) and that momentum bars happen due to high volume. Sure, sometimes this is right, but most of the time momentum bars (liquidity gaps) are thin market moves (low volume) because price has to move in one direction once the last unfilled order is filled and ready to move to the next liquidity zone (base), where enough opposing orders get filled to stop price for some time, until again the balance gets broken one way or the other. This is also the reason why price bounces from those bases, because of unfilled orders left over from the last battle. S/D traders say that those orders at the bases are left there for undefined time, even for years. But it was a real revelation to me what RTM teaches about targets (PAZ). Another common reason for RBD/DBR failures is also explained by RTM. Just by knowing this and the above, we should be able to filter out many losses. Now to what really matters, the context where caps happen. Target 1 was there because of the past history: I see that in the last part I'm already ahead with FTRs, engulfs and targets. I will try to get in those in my next series of posts. And it is also clear from the above, that one concept taken in isolation (in this case price caps) is not enough to decipher price. I hope to be able to do this consistently Journal review: Jurij wrote: NZDCAD DM in play? 4H 30m initial QM spotted by a trading mate, so not all my credit Looking back at this, at that time it was a solid looking setup to me. The problem and the error I've been doing is to consider scales, making everything more complicated than it is, especially mixing smaller and higher scale FTR/FL boxes. But the market doesn't care about boxes with fixed rules (for ex. 4H box is stronger than 5m box and an eng is a signal...). If a 4H FTR/FL box is made as a reaction to a 1m FL it is because of these orders sitting there. Orders have not time frames because they are just orders. There are levels that are stronger than others, not because of time frame but because of orders and decisions of greater or lesser importance (swap levels vs simple barriers...) Thanks to Salivan and Omid I began to focus on the real orders (true supply/demand aka FL) and this was a big missing piece in my analysis Attachments: Check this box to be notified of replies to this topic. In case of EURAUD there was actually a nice setup: Why does this help? Because we know FLs are the edges of a PAZ, the extreme of a zone, so if we get a LTF eng then usually this edge is respected as the intention (signal) was given... "...But FOF is only present with PA, until then it is just unfilled orders that could bounce price " many thanks all the best Salivan explained nicely FOF in his jorunal. Basically unfilled orders are one thing but FOF is different. For example if we have unfilled orders we can expect only a bounce. If we have PA (signal/intention) then the last set of unfilled orders becomes FOF as there are no orders beyond that FOF level. Without the signal, we have just the last set of unfilled orders but no guarantee that the level holds. If the ITs filled all their orders beyond a certain level, it doesn't make sense to fake out past it, they must hate drawdown too... That last level will have all limit orders of the ITs to make sure it doesn't break. Once tg is hit, those orders are removed. And price is allowed to break that level. That's my understanding of FOF as of now and since I'm new to FOF as well, I'm not really sure about it yet. Hope it helps. Check this box to be notified of replies to this topic. First the charts As you can see price stopped at the first opposing FL of that scale (good for 1st profit tg). Then the pivot low 30m FL base, was not a good point for the full reversal. Reasons: 1. the base was a pivot low, which means a reaction to a previous base, in this case a 30m FTR (which itself is the top of a small CP) 2. the sharp arrival and departure makes this more a stop hunt/fake out than a full reversal, also because most reversals have larger tops with QM/diamond levels 3.this low (where my entry was) and the pivot low can be used by ITs for future tricks (FO), whereas that small 30m FTR looks absolutely not interesting to retail traders 4. the better entry can be seen on chart #2 after the new 1m engulf signal either at the 1m quasimodo level or at the origin of the engulf, with the stop below the ftr base, I started to doubt about the validity of that engulf, but in the end price reached the target FL above. All this drama happens in the big picture: From H4 supply to H4 demand (or lower... haven't checked). So basically you were buying where everyone was selling. Now you know. As I already wrote this in the classroom thread few days ago: The FTR is a structure that forms only AFTER a break of a level/zone. The FTR can become a FL when price bounces from it, hence the name (it limits the flag). The flag limit is just a property of the FTR. In one of the first post I wrote that for me a FL is a FTR of a previous FTR (something like an important FTR). Then I had a lot of trouble because of the markepedia FL page which shows FLs before a zone break (ie. FL without FTR). I would call those decision points rather than FLs. But now it is clear to me that there is no FL without FTR. And to clear that confusion, here is now my newest understanding. As I already wrote this in the classroom thread few days ago: The FTR is a structure that forms only AFTER a break of a level/zone. The FTR can become a FL when price bounces from it, hence the name (it limits the flag). The flag limit is just a property of the FTR. Here a chart from IF posted on FF Well yes a FL is the very extreme or the very Limit of a Flag beyond which price just can't go hence it kinda Limits the price beyond that. And basically all FLs are formed because of FTR, because price just can't return to the old price action zone thus again limiting price upto a certain level. But thanks for bringing up this crucial concept for clarification of all in here, and also for referring to that diagram by IF. It says all. Check this box to be notified of replies to this topic. That was an engulf where price DID move to the next FL, but that's all you can reasonably expect since you were on such a low time frame. I think the mistake was expecting price to KEEP going down on such a low time frame move. Usually I try to only use the M1 to validate a higher time frame move. I marked up your chart looking at it more holistically. 1. You see price engulfed what looks to be a fairly significant FL. And it engulfed it with a bull candle (2), which would suggest price wants to go up. At this point I would be looking for an area to enter a long trade. 3. Now price did engulf downward, but it was in the context of a larger move. Price was compressing into the bull candle. At the end of the compression, you would expect price to continue going up. Rather than go short here I would read price is just retracing before continuing its move up. 4. And you see the compression ended right at the s/r flip level, and price continued its move up. The s/r flip level and base of the pole are possible areas to look for a long entry, depending on your risk profile. When starting off, try to stick to the higher time frames for analysis. I bet if you were looking at the m5 or m15, it would have been easier to see that price wanted to move up. Attachments: Check this box to be notified of replies to this topic. Pred!ct0r Report to moderator Quick Reply Reply Quote Thank You Jurij's Corner 29 Mar 2016 00:48 #103 Jurij Topic Author --> Offline Associate Trader Think in terms of frequency Posts: 557 Thank you received: 1348 claudiuschan wrote: Jurij wrote: Psychology of stop hunting Hi Jurij, first of all thanks for the post, it really make me have more understanding on the market direction. Just a quick question, how you know which is the retailer stop? You know all retailers who follow trend put their stop below the last newly formed high/low in expectation for a trend continuation (new high/low). So retailer stops are just beyond pivot highs/lows, but here at RTM we know that the true orders are at the FTRs and those highs/lows are made sometimes to build traps so that ITs take the stops from retailers to get some extra liquidity. In that way, even if they are right on the direction, they lose. The idea with that chart is, once you know the new direction and target price wants to follow, when you see some highs or lows just above/below a fresh FTR then it is likely that price fakes out to the fresh zone. I can conclude from my own experience that the shape of the base and departure strength from a level have only limited influence on the overall outcome. What really matters, as RTM teaches, is the context. But before I get into that. There are some important clues that I consider to determine the quality of the base, I'm sure someone else here at RTM pointed them out. https://www.readthemarket.com/index.php/en/forum/journals/2410-jurij-s-corner 5/58 7/27/2018 Jurij's Corner - RTM Community HOME EDUCATION FORUM MORE LOGOUT An interesting fact is that many traders think that consolidation (bases in RBD/RBD/RBR/DBD) means low activity (volume) and that momentum bars happen due to high volume. Sure, sometimes this is right, but most of the time momentum bars (liquidity gaps) are thin market moves (low volume) because price has to move in one direction once the last unfilled order is filled and ready to move to the next liquidity zone https://www.readthemarket.com/index.php/en/forum/journals/2410-jurij-s-corner 6/58 7/27/2018 Jurij's Corner - RTM Community (base), where enough opposing orders get filled to stop price for some time, until again HOME EDUCATION FORUM MORE LOGOUT the balance gets broken one way or the other. This is also the reason why price bounces from those bases, because of unfilled orders left over from the last battle. S/D traders say that those orders at the bases are left there for undefined time, even for years. But it was a real revelation to me what RTM teaches about targets (PAZ). Another common reason for RBD/DBR failures is also explained by RTM. https://www.readthemarket.com/index.php/en/forum/journals/2410-jurij-s-corner 7/58 7/27/2018 Jurij's Corner - RTM Community HOME EDUCATION FORUM MORE LOGOUT Just by knowing this and the above, we should be able to filter out many losses.
